blocks.x: I've affiliated with him off in the hall for about 50 years. Maybe we should move this a little closer. Kirk, you can move that a little closer. He ain't what he used to be. He ain't what he used to be. Who do you mean, Heish? Domo or Neto. They say that the first thing you lose when you're 80 years old is your...
Yeah, we got the second reel up right now.
Where was I?
You want to get back to where we were?
Yeah, I suppose.
We were at the Marigold and the guy was having problems with money.

Yeah, well, he liked to get an extra $75 to go to have his wife have his first child. And so we went up there and played an audition, I don't remember the fellow's name, but and he says how many, we played several tunes for him over there, Ain't She Sweet and those kind of tunes which was popular in those days, and the guy, and I was playing trumpet, and I went out there and the guy said how many tunes do you know? He says, I said well we can write down and we'll play 46 tunes for you. I didn't know we were at 46 or not, he said well it'd be 46 before you repeat one, you know, you play two choruses and they'd collect the dance, the Ten Cents to Dance, and then then as soon as you see them all walk off the floor there, you'd sort the next tune and play two choruses, I would do you remember that Godfrey over there from the fine. And so we took the job for two weeks. Then he wanted to keep us the third week, but before I said no, and I said I want to go. Well around the second week there, Al Streeman come over there and he spoke to me, he says, I said would you be interested to play a night in a hotel next week, in the Roosevelt Hotel? And I said with the Isles Orchestra, I never heard of the Isles Orchestra, I didn't know anything about them. And I said well how much do they pay? He says ten dollars. I said ten dollars? We were getting thirty bucks a week to play seven days a week down there. And I said ten dollars? I said yeah I'll take it. So I went over there and Bill Padron got his tooth pulled and I played the night for him. And Al Crumb come to me and he says, you know we're non-union. And he says we have an agreement with the boss over here, which was Mike Moss running the Roosevelt at the time. And he says that as long as you stay non-union you'll have a job. But if you join the union, out you go. So he says we'd like to add a trombone to the band. I said well, I said I played trombone in the service. I said, he said well can you get a horn? I went to the Boyle Islands and borrowed it from Brownlee, you remember Brownlee, Godfrey? I borrowed it from Brownlee and I told him, I said look, I said if I take the job, I said I'll buy a horn for you. So he loaned me the horn and I went to play there, it was Halloween night. The year, I don't know whether it was, you remember what year it would be? 25, 26?
This was before the Owls recorded?

No, they made one recording. Pardon me for interrupting you for just a second, these names came to my mind just now. Warren Herron was the drummer with Johnny Tobin's band and Bonnie Pottle was the bass player. Yeah, that's right, Bonnie Pottle.
Very fine bass player.
In fact he worked with us when I was with him at the Edgewater Beach Hotel. Yeah, Bonnie Pottle. In 1940. In fact I think he committed suicide. So go ahead, I'm sorry, Bonnie Pottle.
So this was 25 or 26? Halloween.

Yeah, yeah, Halloween night. And Mike Moss, he's big up there with his glass eye. I didn't know he had a glass eye. And when you look at a glass eye, it's always looking at you, you know? So I thought it was looking at me all the time. So Earl Crumb, after the night was over the next day, he says, well, the job is yours. He says, I hope you take it. I said, well, I will take it. Earl Crumb was leader then at that point. Yeah, he was the manager. He was the leader. He wasn't the leader, he was the manager. The manager. It was his. We rehearsed without a drum. Because they didn't do too much reading. In fact I think I was about the best reader in the band. In fact I'm pretty sure of that.
And who was the bass player? Dan LeBlanc, his tuba. Well Dan was a good reader. But not that much.

Yeah, he, you know those tuba players, as you well know, you know. You start to give them a violin sheet, you know, or something like that. It's kind of a little fast one. That's like Jumbo used to tell me. He looked at my part over there when he was playing some of those stuff over there. He says, well, none of these guys around here can play that part. He says, they can't read that fast. I said, well, hell, that's not that fast. I said, after all, they played the trombone over there. You get some fast stuff on the trombone. So anyway, I went there and I stayed with the Owls until they disbanded. And actually the disbanding of it was when we left the Edgewater Hotel. That's when we got Eddie Miller and... Bill Padron. Well Bill Padron stayed with us. He was with the band. In fact Bill Padron and René Jelper I think. And the later years, the last two years I think they had Pinky. But they started off with seven then.
Well Pinky was with the Owls for quite a while.
Yeah, well I know, but Pinky came in after I did. I joined before Pinky. Because he was out at the roof.
Huh? He was out at the roof.
Yeah, I know. The first season...
He was on the records. He was on the records.
Yeah. The first season they made the Owls hoot. And several other, whatever that session was. I wasn't in that. That was... That you worked to.
Yeah.
That was... I joined them right after that. And the other...
You have some Owls records here? Oh yeah.

I'm not going to hear... We made some recording. We made some up there in the Gacho building there. Or I think it was the Gacho building. Yeah. Gacho building. Yeah. Gacho building. That's where it was. Gacho building. And then we went to Atlanta to make that other trip. And I think that's... With them, that's the only recording I made. Because I made some wood.
Jack Yates was in that building. I think you did in Jack Yates's studio. Yeah.
Really? I don't know.
I think you did in the...
But I was on bass then.
In Jack Yates's studio up there. Jack Yates.

And Von Gammon was the drummer then. Yeah. Von Gammon and Von had a nose for money, boy. And as you know, Perranti, he wouldn't pay anybody. So he rang me up one morning over. He says, come on. He says, we're going to make a recording session. And I said, okay. So Von Gammon says, go ahead. Come on over there. He says, we'll go. No, no, no tune. No name. No nothing. I don't know. It was just started off. E flat. Start off. And Perranti started playing. And he had Charlie Hartman on trombone. And he had Von Gammon on drums. Oh boy, where's the rest of it going? You know, there's a funny thing. Oh yeah. Who was that piano player that... Joe Wolf? No, not Joe Wolf was the other... Might have been Joe. From New York?
He was from New York? No, no.
It was a piano player that used to work more or less by himself down back in those days. Could have been Joe Wolf.
Was he in the band after Witt Lubowski? Witt Lubowski...

Oh, Witt. Witt was in the sang. No, Witt was... Witt went to the little club, didn't he? Witt was... Witt was... Witt was... Now this is getting in my era. Witt was at the Liberty Theatre. At the Liberty Theatre they had Witt Lubowski on piano. They had Tony Perranti on... Tony Papalia was on saxophone.
Witt played drums.

Witt played drums. And I can't... Frank... I can't remember the piano player's name. Well, I'm sure... Witt Lubowski. I'm sure... Witt went... Witt did go to the sang. You're right. Witt did go to the sang at the theatre before he died. Yeah, yeah. In fact, I used to go out with his wife after... Shame on her.
No, after he died.
Hazel, Hazel Lubowski, I mean... Yeah, Hazel. She married... That was a saxophone. She married Johnny Sabre. Yeah.
She married Johnny Sabre. She married Johnny Sabre.
Well, who... Henry Raymond said... Yeah.
No, I mean, it was...
This was no cheap affair. I mean, it was... Did you take it down to your studio? Did you take it down to your studio? No, no, no, no.

You ought to see that. Not Hazel. I was in there. I got a key from him over there. No, no, no, no. He had 700 keys there. If the red light was on, don't come in. If the red light was on. He'll come back later. Well, I think Tony had left the Liberty then.
When Von Gatwood... Could you tell me? Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, it was a little club. Oh, yeah. Well, that was Tony Denapolis' place. Yeah.
That was up on Verone Street. Yeah.
That was on Common and... At first it was Common. Then they moved up on Verone Street.
Common and O'Keefe. Yeah.
Yeah. Then they moved up there to around 700, 800 block of Verone Street. Across from that.
Yeah. But then Tony didn't run it then. That was when his brother... Who was the other...

Uh-huh. ...the other sort of master ceremonies up to Denapolis? Who, George McQueen? No, no. It was Denapolis. Tony's brother. I don't know. Tony was... Nightclub operators. So you were playing bass when you did that session? Oh, yeah. I was playing bass. So that wasn't the thing. Yeah.
I was playing bass.
Yeah. I was playing bass.
So that was in the 30s, huh? Yeah, that was just about the 30s, yeah.
It had to be, yeah, because...
That was before I went out to the 25 Cent Club with Eddie Miller, Armand Hug, Bill Padron.
It was a 25 Cent Club with the 25 Cent Club across the...
From the Hunnysuckle Inn.
Yeah. Yeah. And then when it took Cherokee's job away from him at Hunnysuckle Inn when Hip couldn't
play or sing. Well who was... Who was... Who was... Who was...
Who was... Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
Who was...
his job away from him at the honeysuckle inn when hip couldn't play as well.
Who owned the 25 cent club? Hip Kinley and the two Pettengels.
That's where I worked. Yeah you started to work in that too.

But we were playing at the honeysuckle when you were in there weren't you? I think you were. Yeah we were playing. Because this is funny. This is a funny thing. There's a road there that comes down from one road. One house is here. Actually, Pontchartrain Boulevard. There was a Pan Am gas station in the corner. In about two blocks. It's actually Avenue A. I was in a house which is at one time the honeysuckle inn. This lady owned because I had a hospital bed.
Old Man Myers used to rent the rooms for a while.

So this was after it was redone. After it was all redone from the nightclub. And they used to have this road coming down there. And they had guys from the two bits club and from the honeysuckle inn. They had these lanterns. Lans. Kerosene lanterns. You know like a railroad lantern like that. You could swing it like that. And they're flagging you in for the white picture. And they're flagging you in. And they're flagging you in to come to their place. Well, if the honeysuckle inn was first and the band would start, man, Randazzo, the waiter. Yeah.
Sam Randazzo.

They all asked for you. Yeah, yeah, yeah. The cow's ass, the chicken's ass. And by the minute the automobile passed by the honeysuckle inn to go over to the two bits club. And they'd go over to the two bits club. Stop. And if somebody would come in there, if they were the first couple to come in there after the air and all this stuff, they'd walk in there and the place is empty and nothing's happening. And they couldn't figure it out.

They used to put the ice in hot bowls and put the bowls in the oven and the ice was two bits of bowl. Two bits of bowl. So they'd melt. There was no liquor in those days. That was prohibition. And the only thing they could get was two bits for the bowl of ice. So they'd get that hot bowl out there.
Sandwich was two bits, a Coke was two bits, and everything was two bits.
They'd get that hot bowl out the oven, fill it with ice, and put it on the table. And if you got up to dance, 20 seconds, you had nothing but water. And that was it.
It was funny enough.
Do you remember Johnny Detroit's band, Cobbs? That was one.

Yes, we were playing with the Owls then when Johnny was at Cub. It was El Straticus and he had, who else was with El Straticus and... Well his brother probably, Paul. Probably Paul, yeah, his brother on drums. And now who... Probably Tony Peretti.
Huh? Probably Tony Peretti would be...
Well Tony Peretti had his own band most of the time.
He worked with Johnny quite often.
I know he did. Well they switched around when they had the job, you know. Tony would get...
Where were you, say where they working then? With what they...
Well they worked at Cobbs. At Cobbs, yeah. On a couple of different occasions. I don't remember. They started out in the late teens working at Cobbs. I don't remember.
Johnny Peretti. Yeah, he worked in there during the carnival season. It wasn't a steady job through that. I mean I don't... Now Cobbs, when they started... Fulco played in Cobbs straight on for...
Well he was in Cobbs with Sandy and... Yeah, with Sandy and Joe Schultz and...
And playing string music. Yeah, playing string music in Cobbs. Who is Sandy?

Sandy was a cello player. Manuel Perez Sandy. I know, you're right. And he had a lot of... He had a lot of children that were unclaimed and illegitimate. And so one day I asked him very seriously. I says, Manuel, I says, how many illegitimate children do you have? And I knew that they had at least five of them. He says, do you mean in the United States or Mexico? He was very proud. He let them know that. It was the United States or Mexico.
Johnny's Detroit's band played the tea dances up on the second floor. At Cobbs?
Well, no, I can't go back there for one more time. Johnny just died about a year. I can't remember that. I can't remember that. Johnny was 90s some more.

Johnny always had the great ambition to have an orchestra. In fact, Johnny was at the Roseveld Hotel Fountain Grill. No, he was in a cave. In the cave. No, no, before or after that. Because my daddy was his substitute player. Was that after us or before us? I don't know. That was before you. Well, I... It was the Fountain Grill was where the coffee shop, where Bailey's is today. You know where Bailey's is? Coming out on Burk and Harone Street. Yeah, I remember that.
I remember that.

And my father substituted for Johnny Detroit for so many weeks while he went to New York, when Johnny went to New York. Yeah, but I didn't know he would. And he was a very dear friend of my father's. Whenever Johnny would talk to me about my daddy, he never stopped. He thought my daddy was the greatest thing in the world.
I remember your daddy quite well too. With his fly on and the other man, the immaculate. He had two suits.
He had 11 suits.
One on and one off. And he had that big old automobile that was a half a block long sitting over there. You think he was a millionaire. You think he was a millionaire, believe me.

That's right. The old man was immaculate. I never saw my father at any time in his life without a collar and tie on. In those days, he used to wear collars where he had to put a collar button on and another collar on top of you.
You remember the Beisdorfer band, I take it, huh?

I remember Johnny Beisdorf. I played with him several, not steady, several incidental jobs. Uh-huh. But, uh, now all of this is on base. That's all after. Because when depression hit, I think I went about 14 months without a, with a $5 job.
Do you remember the Beisdorfer band back in the period when you were coming out of the Navy?

I heard of it. I heard of it, yeah. I heard of it. I heard of it when I came. Is that the one that was at the Toque T out at Spanish Fort? It's at Spanish Fort, yeah. Yeah. I used to listen. My father played with Pal Eddie's band, which used to be the concert band out there.

And he used to take me out there in the afternoon. Well, that was at West End Park. No, no, no. At Spanish Fort? Spanish Fort, yeah. Spanish Fort. I didn't think Pal Eddie went to Spanish Fort. Yeah, he was at Spanish Fort.
And we used to go, I used to go out there in the afternoon with my daddy and I'd get lost

from listening to the military band and I'd go over and listen to Johnny Beisdorf, his jazz band. I believe that. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I was a band. I never did get in. Well, I was in Tokyo Garden. Tokyo, Tokyo Tea, Tokyo Tea Gardens. Yeah. And I never got the chance. I never got inside to hear. Tokyo Tea is Tokyo. Geez. The first alto player that was with Joe Furco at the Lowest State was the first alto sax, Italian boy. Oh, not the great one.
No. Before Skaggs? Skaggioni. Skaggioni.
Skaggioni. Oh yeah. Skaggioni. Skaggioni. Skaggioni. Skaggioni. Skaggioni. He was with him out there. Do you remember the Badukes? Oh yeah.

I played with Jews in the rave. I swear to God, I don't know how the hell he ever, he was the worst drummer I ever played with. I swear before God. Never could keep tempo. But he threw the sticks up in the air and he jigged and everything else. But he's still playing too. Oh yeah, he sure is. He's still there.
He's in Houston. He's in Houston.
Yeah, he's in Houston. When did you play with Ray? With Jules. You played with Jules? Yeah, I played with Jules.

I played there with that, what was that place on the highway, on Clavin Avenue up there? Remember that place? What the hell they called? We used to put some Jacks programs on up there. How far up was it? Not too far, it was past where, it was past the roadways. Oh, up in Jefferson. Yeah, yeah, up in Jefferson. Thomas C's joint. Thomas C was at our end.
Thomas C was over across the river. Huh? Evans Thomas C was across the river.
Now wait a minute, he was on this side.
Midway, Evans Thomas C was midway. Well, who had this place on this side of the river? From Napoleon Avenue Ferry. Huh?
No, this place on this side of the river, don't you know? They rented the cabins in the back there for...
Oh, I know what you were talking about.
Cotton Club?
Yeah, they're right across the street from where the Arrow Room used to be.
Cotton Club. Near the Cotton Club? Yeah, I think that was it, the Cotton Club. Sure, that was it. Not the Blue Horseshoe.

No, no, no. Cotton Club. No, the Cotton Club. Blue Horseshoe. Blue Horseshoe was backed by the... Yeah, that was it, the Cotton Club. Blue Horseshoe used to be backed by the Two Bits Club in the... What's in the... Where you were. And that was where Farzola used to go all the time. In fact, one morning we were playing the theme song, the WWL, and... I don't know whether it's just good to put on or not. He's leaving the... They're just playing the theme and Farz walks out of the studio and Ed Hernan says, where are you going? He says, I gotta go out the Blue Horseshoe. I remember that my girlfriend left her teeth on the windowsill. I gotta go pick him up.
You got the right name. Cotton Club, that's it.
That's it.
Yeah, you were at the Cotton Club?
I was with Jules Baduc. Jules Baduc. Yeah, Jules. Ray was at that time was with Crosby, Bob Crosby. Jules had a very good band down there on Bourbon Street.
You remember when...

I worked with him down there where Jumbo's joint is today. I played with him down there and I made an audition for that job. And I was working in there with Ray McNamara. I think... And he come and got me to audition for a job. He said, do me a favor. Do me a favor. Do me a favor. He says, I want to make an audition for a guy. In fact, Joe Massara. When I went in there and made the place over there, we were hoisting in another place. And who walks in there is Joe Massara. I says, for Christ's sake, I'm working for the guy right now. I said... And I went and met to McNamara that night. I said, Ray, I said, I auditioned for my own job over here. He says, well, take it. He says, I ain't gonna stay in this place anyway. He says, I'm sick and tired of it.
Do you remember when Ray worked for Beiersdorfer?

When Ray... Ray Paduca. Ray Paduca. Ray Paduca. Ray Paduca. Yeah, he was out there on the lakefront. Yeah, yeah. He was... Ray was quite young. How old is he now? Would you give an idea? He's gotta be 80 years old. He's 80.
Yeah, he just turned 80. He just turned 80.

Well, I thought he was a couple of years younger than me. But Ray, we thought half a time, a dozen times over. After Crum got finished, we didn't know him. Excuse me. I'm sorry, Ray. If you ever hear this.
We'll restrict that. He wasn't. Yeah. He wasn't the best liked drummer in the world. No, no. His personality, he didn't have a...

He didn't have a big personality. He jigged and he threw the sticks up in the air. He was a clown. And today, he would probably be terrific. Who were the drummers that you did like? I liked Pothead Addy. I liked Von Gammon. Von Gammon. And there was two.
I played drums with us.

Listen, children do it. I played drums with us. I know you played drums too. I played drums with you too. Yeah, but you played drums with us too, but not very long. You were playing mostly piano and the... No, I played drums at the radio station. Huh? I played drums at the radio station. Yeah, I know. I was a premier percussionist down there. That's right. That's right.
But you were playing vibes up there. You were talking or you were playing piano. . . . .

. . . . There's a funny thing about your comrades there, your, what the hell do you call them, your Jewish friends. He's playing vibes over there and the guy comes over there with his hand and grabs you and saying, how you doing, Godfrey? And here's the guy playing a chorus on the vibes. He did that the other night. Who the hell was that Levy guy? Yeah, I don't know. Yeah, they go up there, he's playing the tune over there, I don't remember what the tune was, and he's going along there and the guy comes up and he sees Godfrey and Godfrey knows all those Jews up there, you know the question about it, and they come over there to shake hands with him. The man's playing a good kid, waiting until he's finished. He's got to grab his hand there and Godfrey's got to put the other one down and there is Ken Carr and I. I didn't stop playing. You know, Ken says, Frank, he says, did you know we had a two piece van up here?
That's the trouble I get for booking a three piece job.
Yeah, well, no, the job was alright, there was nothing wrong with the job. They don't talk to you when you're not playing.
That's right. Well, I know too many of those people, I knew all of them. In fact, I was... Well, you went to school with all of them. I went to school with half of them.
So when you were with the Owls at the hotel, you couldn't be Union. When did you join the Union?
We joined the Union when we went to the Edgewater Club. Edgewater Beach Hotel. So you've been in the Union then since the late 20s, huh? Edgewater Golf. Yeah, 28. 28, 29. It's Edgewater Golf Hotel.
Edgewater Golf Hotel, yeah.
That was... We went over there, that's when we got Hilton Lamar and we got... Who else? I believe that was the only one that... Yeah, Rene went... Rene Jalopy went to the Tudeling.
That's when Earl was starting to learn how to read and they were playing some overture and he went to...

I was playing fiddle up there. We had to make a concert up there. We had an hour, a half hour, an hour dinner session and Earl says, go get a violin someplace, you're going to have to play violin in there. So we played a few tunes over there and they had time for a cymbal beat and I told Earl, I said, just hold your hand in there, I'll tell you when it comes and I'll hold on in it. And when I told him now, he pulls it and there's an electric fan up there and he gets a hand hooked in the fan and down comes the electric fan. And it did get the cymbal beat.
Earl couldn't read that. He couldn't read a note as big as a...

Earl was playing the Vulgar Boatman over there and here comes Hilton Lamar with the guitar, he's not playing in the orchestra and he's carrying a little handmade paper boat in front of that band and he's lugging along and the Vulgar Boatman is coming on in front of there. How the hell can you play? I'll tell you Pinky though, Pinky was fabulous at putting on those police shows, you get on and put that continuity out there, you couldn't play. You just had a laugh at him. There was no question about that.

Well the funny thing about the police shows was that these guys, and this is the most ridiculous thing of all, Wiley Harris who was one of the promoters of the show, every year they had to take a trip to the Edgewater Beach Hotel to hear the band to see if it would be acceptable to play for the police PMBA, Police Mutual Benefit Association. And he and a couple of other guys would have to go up to Chicago to hear the band to see if it was alright for them. Regardless of who it was, this band was coming to the Roosevelt Hotel and that was the band that they were going to get whether they liked it or not because that's the band that Seymour Weiss gave it to him. And he said, he said, Seymour Weiss set a, what do you call it, I can't remember, a statue before by leaving the band off to play Monday night for the PMBA, the Roosevelt Hotel Orchestra. I mean the band that was playing at the Roosevelt. They would give him permission to go up there and play that show, it was alright for the union to give him that. But if the band wanted to play another job, the band that was on a job like Kellner's band or any of the other bands that wanted to have a, that there was a night off that they could play another job, they wouldn't allow it. And I think there was an unjust situation with the whole thing.
I got a note here that says something about double headliner bill. Oh yeah, I found that on the newspaper. What was the double headliner bill, do you know, in a theater, like in Vaudeville?

Oh yeah, double headliner, you had two feature pictures. Oh I see. Yeah, you had two feature pictures. Oh, so that had nothing to do with the band. No, no, no, no, no. The band would be in between each one of them. Oh, in between the, oh yeah.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. And they mentioned the four Camerons.
Do you remember that act?
I remember the name. Yeah. But I couldn't, I couldn't. Well it, it, I found the thing in the newspaper, it had quite a write up on the, on that.

Yeah, well the double feature was, that was two, two, two full, full pictures. Oh, double feature, it's like that. Yeah, two, two out pictures. Did I tell you? Incidentally, Charlie Duke was a good drummer. Yeah. I liked him. Charlie Pager, your good solid tempo. And anytime you played the good solid tempo, I liked it. You do too. That's right. I was one of his parmars. I was one of his parmars. What about Ferdinand Trombino? That's, that's another story. I never will forget Joe Loi Canna playing saxophone on there.
And I was one of his parmars. I was one of his parmars. What about Ferdinand Trombino?

That's, that's another story. I never will forget Joe Loi Canna playing saxophone on there. And he comes in there and if you saw, he had one leg. And if Joe wouldn't cross the river for nothing in a well, he wasn't going to cross the river. If you had a job on there to give a damn it for what it was, he wasn't going to cross it. And then we go to work at the Silver Slipper down at the... That's what I was trying to remember. That's where Jules Paduca was at the Silver Slipper. Yeah, he was down there too. But I wasn't with him there. He went down in the Silver Slipper and Joe Loi Canna was sitting down there playing saxophone. We worked from 10.30 to 4.30, I believe, for that 30 bucks a week or 35 dollars a week. And seven nights a week. And Ferdinand Firmino comes in there and the first night, I believe, on the job, we come down there and he says, Boys, you're going to have your dinner. And I sat down there and they had pigtails. And I never had eight pigtails in my life. I don't know. I said, what the hell is that? And he said, boys, enjoy your dinner. He says, your meals on the house, you know. And Joe Loi Canna says, yeah. He says, I know you feed hog slop and they get fat. He told that to get that big. Trambino, he was the owner of the place, huh? Yeah, he was the manager, I think. Judge, what you called him? I remember that night court judge. The night court judge?
Yeah, you told us about him last night. LeBlanc, Judge LeBlanc? No, no.

Hammer. Hammer, Judge Hammer. Judge Hammer, he owned the joint over there. Then his brother-in-law took Ferdinand Trambino's place. DeFranco. Tony DeFranco. Tony DeFranco. Tony DeFranco. You can't put this on the tape, I'll tell you, because when Abby Brunus was down there playing on the job, and Tony come in loaded, laying. Did I put that on the tape last time? No. No. He come down there, and he's laying on the floor, and Tony had a terrific nose. Oh, the woman. The woman, yeah. Yeah, the woman goes over there, and she's gorgeous, absolutely. She was beautiful. That was his girlfriend. And he took him down there, and she'd heard about him going out with some blonde. This was a black-headed gal. And she looked at him, and she says, you dirty, no good. MF, and you SOB, and everything else, and all the boys over there.
